steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper on learning high-level semantic-relational concepts (Rooms and Walls) for SLAM with graph neural networks, integrated into S-Graphs+. Motivate semantic-relational entities, review 3D scene graph work, explain the limitation we address and our approach, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why high-level semantic-relational entities matter for robots
- 3D scene graphs and related real-time work
- S-Graphs+ and the limitation of hand-tuned entity extraction
- Our GNN-based framework for generating Rooms and Walls
- Synthetic training data and results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - semantic-relational entities -> situational awareness (cite), richer world model, scene understanding
  - helps later tasks: planning (cite), robot navigation (cite)
- 3D scene graphs (cite)
  - promising framework for semantic-relational modelling of the scene
  - one work (cite): relations between observed objects in real time, but no new entities
  - Hydra (cite): builds and optimizes 3D scene graph in real time, loop closures
- S-Graphs+ (cite)
  - tighter coupling: four-layered optimizable factor graph = SLAM graph + 3D scene graph (Fig. 1)
  - lowest layer: robot Keyframes; second: raw geometric entities, Planes (vertical planes called Walls in (cite))
  - upper two layers: scene graph, Room entities linked to Planes, Floor entities linked to Rooms
  - limitation: Hydra (cite) and S-Graphs+ (cite) use ad-hoc hand-tuned algorithms for Rooms/Floors -> not generalizable to complex, irregular indoor environments
- Our framework
  - learn to generate semantic entities with GNNs (cite)
  - improve Room generation + new entities like Walls (two parallel vertical planes), common architecture
  - observed entities -> proximity graph -> message passing (Fig. 1)
  - GNN classifies nodes into same Room / same Wall / none; clustering using cycles
  - per cluster: new Room or Wall node + factors coupling to Planes
  - nodes and factors back into S-Graphs+ (cite)
- Data and results
  - synthetic dataset as ground truth graph: Planes, Rooms, Walls, relations
  - no fine-tuning; simulated and real structured indoor environments
  - better than baselines in detection time, expressiveness, number of entities
- Contributions
  - GNN-based framework for Rooms/Walls + relations to Planes: precise, fast, versatile
  - integration into S-Graphs+ (cite), validation on simulated and real datasets, ablations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
High-level semantic-relational entities improve the situational awareness of a robot and make the built world model richer, which improves scene understanding. They also give useful information for later tasks such as planning or robot navigation.

In recent years 3D Scene Graphs have become a promising framework for modelling the scene with semantic-relational concepts. Another work goes a step further and generates the relations between observed objects in real time, but it does not include new entities. Hydra builds and optimizes the 3D scene graph in real time, using loop closures.

S-Graphs+ couples them more tightly and generates a four-layered optimizable factor graph that contains a SLAM graph and a 3D scene graph, as shown in Fig. 1. The lowest layer of the graph has the robot Keyframes, which are connected to the second layer. The second layer is made of directly observed raw geometric entities, i.e. Planes (vertical planes, which are named Walls in the S-Graphs+ work). The upper two layers are a scene graph, with semantic Room entities related to the underlying Planes and semantic Floor entities connected to their Rooms. But Hydra and S-Graphs+ extract the semantic Room and Floor entities with ad-hoc hand-tuned algorithms, so they do not generalize to complex and irregularly shaped indoor environments.

- Our framework
  - learn to generate semantic entities with GNNs (cite); better Room generation + new Walls entities, common architecture
  - observed entities -> proximity graph -> message passing (Fig. 1)
  - node classes same Room / same Wall / none; clustering using cycles; new Room/Wall nodes + factors to Planes
  - back into S-Graphs+ (cite) for semantic-relational SLAM
- Synthetic training dataset (Planes, Rooms, Walls, relations); no fine-tuning; simulated + real environments; better detection time, expressiveness, number of entities
- Contributions: GNN framework; integration into S-Graphs+ (cite) with validation and ablations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
High-level semantic-relational entities improve the situational awareness of a robot and make the built world model richer, which improves scene understanding. They also give useful information for later tasks such as planning or robot navigation.

In recent years 3D Scene Graphs have become a promising framework for modelling the scene with semantic-relational concepts. Another work goes a step further and generates the relations between observed objects in real time, but it does not include new entities. Hydra builds and optimizes the 3D scene graph in real time, using loop closures.

S-Graphs+ couples them more tightly and generates a four-layered optimizable factor graph that contains a SLAM graph and a 3D scene graph, as shown in Fig. 1. The lowest layer of the graph has the robot Keyframes, which are connected to the second layer. The second layer is made of directly observed raw geometric entities, i.e. Planes (vertical planes, which are named Walls in the S-Graphs+ work). The upper two layers are a scene graph, with semantic Room entities related to the underlying Planes and semantic Floor entities connected to their Rooms. But Hydra and S-Graphs+ extract the semantic Room and Floor entities with ad-hoc hand-tuned algorithms, so they do not generalize to complex and irregularly shaped indoor environments.

To deal with these limitations, we present a framework that improves the relational and generalization capabilities of 3D scene graphs by learning to generate semantic entities with GNNs. With this we improve the state of the art of Room generation, and we also generate new entities such as Walls (two parallel vertical planes), all with a common architecture. As Fig. 1 shows, the observed entities are turned into a proximity graph that is used for message passing. The GNN classifies the type of each node into the concepts same Room, same Wall or none, and these are then processed and clustered using the existence of cycles. For each cluster a new Room or Wall node is generated, together with the factors that couple it tightly to the underlying Planes. The nodes and factors are put back into S-Graphs+ to validate how useful they are for semantic-relational SLAM.

To have a ground truth graph for training the GNN model, we first generate a synthetic dataset with low-level entities, i.e. Planes, and higher-level semantic entities, i.e. Rooms and Walls, together with their relationships. Without any more fine-tuning of the trained GNN model, the results on several simulated and real structured indoor environments show that our method improves on the baselines in detection time, expressiveness and number of detected entities.

The main contributions of our paper are:

- • A GNN-based framework that generates high-level semantic entities (i.e. Rooms and Walls) and their relationships with the low-level entities (i.e. Planes) in a precise, fast and versatile way.

- • Integration of the algorithm in the four-layered optimizable S-Graphs+ framework, with validation on simulated and real datasets and relevant ablations.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
High-level semantic-relational entities enhance a robot’s situational awareness [2] and enrich the built world model, improving scene understanding. They also provide advantageous information for subsequent tasks such as planning [3] or robot navigation [4].

In recent years, 3D Scene Graphs [5,6] have emerged as a promising framework for modelling the scene using semantic-relational concepts. Notably, [7] takes a step further by generating the relations between observed objects in real time, although it does not include new entities. Hydra [8] constructs and optimizes the 3D scene graph in real time, leveraging loop closures.

Coupling them more tightly, S-Graphs+ [1] generates a four-layered optimizable factor graph comprising a SLAM graph and a 3D scene graph, as depicted in Fig. 1. The lowest layer contains the robot Keyframes, connected to the second layer, which is composed of directly observed raw geometric entities, i.e. Planes (vertical planes named Walls in [1]). The upper two layers represent a scene graph containing semantic Room entities related to the underlying Planes and semantic Floor entities connected to the respective Rooms. However, Hydra [8] and S-Graphs+ [1] extract these semantic Room and Floor entities using ad-hoc hand-tuned algorithms, which do not generalize to complex and irregularly shaped indoor environments.

To address these limitations, we present a framework that enhances the relational and generalization capabilities of 3D scene graphs by learning to generate semantic entities with GNNs [9,10]. With it, we not only improve the state of the art of Room generation but also generate new entities such as Walls (two parallel vertical planes), all with a common architecture. As shown in Fig. 1, the observed entities are transformed into a proximity graph used for message passing. The GNN classifies each node into the concepts of same Room, same Wall or none, which are then processed and clustered leveraging the existence of cycles. For each cluster, a new Room or Wall node is generated along with the factors that tightly couple it with the underlying Planes. The nodes and factors are incorporated back into S-Graphs+ [1] to validate their usefulness for semantic-relational SLAM.

As a ground truth graph for training the GNN model, we first generate a synthetic dataset comprising low-level entities, i.e. Planes, and higher-level semantic entities, i.e. Rooms and Walls, along with their relationships. Without further fine-tuning of the trained GNN model, results over several simulated and real structured indoor environments demonstrate that our method improves on the baselines in detection time, expressiveness, and the number of entities detected.

To summarize, the main contributions of our paper are:

- • A GNN-based framework to generate high-level semantic entities (i.e. Rooms and Walls) and their relationships with low-level entities (i.e. Planes) in a precise, fast, and versatile manner.

- • Integration of the algorithm into the four-layered optimizable S-Graphs+ framework [1], with validation in simulated and real datasets and relevant ablations.
